hypothesis_cards.claim: the billing engine's internal 'revenue' field is computed as cash collected at invoice time rather than as an accrual-based recognition schedule, conflating two distinct accounting concepts under one field name
conditions: any consumer of the 'revenue' field assumes it means recognized revenue rather than cash collected
discriminating_information: a case where cash collected and recognized revenue diverge for reasons other than proration timing
hypothesis_cards.falsifier: revenue timing does not actually depend on cash-vs-accrual distinction here
hypothesis_cards.mechanism: the schema was designed around 'money received' as the simplest single source of truth, so anything downstream (dashboards, exports) that reads 'revenue' is actually reading a cash-collection timestamp, not a recognition-period allocation
hypothesis_cards.predicted_readout: separating a distinct 'cash_collected' field from a computed 'recognized_revenue_schedule' field removes the conflation at the source

two_question_intake.q1_answer_verbatim: Every time a customer upgrades their subscription mid-billing-cycle, the billing engine immediately books the full new-plan amount as revenue on the upgrade date, instead of spreading it across the remaining service period. The monthly close team has to manually adjust dozens of entries by hand every month because the general ledger and the engineering team's MRR dashboard never agree.
two_question_intake.q2_answer_verbatim: Have engineering just prorate the upgrade charge by days remaining in the billing cycle before sending it to the ledger.
